title: Steer Like the LLM: Activation Steering that Mimics Prompting
claim: Desired steering interventions can be measured as activation differences under prompting, then approximated by a lightweight model of token-specific coefficients times a fixed vector.
layout: 3 regions, left-to-right; activation difference in center, dashed PSR box on right
description: The figure reads left to right. On the left, two stacked rows of tokens show unsteered activations (red x tokens followed by black y' tokens) and prompt-steered activations (purple x' tokens followed by the same black y' tokens). Above each row, a rounded gray box holds small arrows that show activation vectors per token, red for unsteered and purple for prompt-steered. Both feed into a circled minus operator, which produces a center box of blue arrows. That box is labeled with the Δ_PS equation, A_{y'_i|PS} − A_{y'_i}. A dashed 'If attr ∈ y'' curve links it by an approximately-equals sign to a dashed box on the right labeled PSR Model. That box contains a function λ(A; θ_attr) that outputs blue bar-chart steering coefficients. These are multiplied (⊗) by a blue steering vector z_attr. A long arrow runs from the unsteered activations to the λ box.
caption: Illustration of how prompt steering interventions $\Delta_{PS}$ can be computed by subtracting prompt-steered activations from the corresponding unsteered activations (left and center). Prompt Steering Replacement (PSR) models approximate these interventions, but only on cases where prompt steering successfully elicits the target attribute (right).
abstract: Large language models can be steered at inference time through prompting or activation interventions, but activation steering methods often underperform compared to prompt-based approaches. We propose a framework that formulates prompt steering as a form of activation steering and investigates whether distilling successful prompt steering behavior into simpler, interpretable models can close this gap. Our analysis reveals that popular activation steering methods are not faithful to the mechanics of prompt steering, which applies strong interventions on some tokens while barely affecting others. Based on these insights, we introduce Prompt Steering Replacement (PSR) models that estimate token-specific steering coefficients from the activations themselves and are trained to imitate prompt-based interventions. Experiments on three steering benchmarks across multiple language models show that PSR models outperform existing activation steering methods, especially when controlling for high-coherence completions, and also compare favorably to prompting on AxBench and persona steering.
